name: Luchi
subtitle: small white maida puris that puff into balloons, the sunday-morning bread

ingredients.note: plain white flour — atta makes a puri, not a luchi
the moyan, which keeps the luchi tender

prepNotes: Rub the ghee into the flour first and check it — a fistful should hold its shape when squeezed. That is the correct amount of moyan.
Knead to a dough firmer than chapati dough, then rest it covered with a damp cloth for 20 minutes.
Roll all the luchis out before you start frying and keep them under a cloth; frying goes too fast to roll between batches.

steps.text: Mix the maida, salt and sugar, then rub in the ghee with your fingertips for 2 minutes until it looks like damp sand.
Add the lukewarm water a little at a time and knead 6-8 minutes into a smooth, firm, non-sticky dough.
steps.tip: A soft dough will soak up oil. Luchi dough should feel tight, almost stubborn.

steps.text: Divide into 20 balls the size of a large marble and roll each into a 9cm circle, greasing the board with a drop of oil rather than dusting with flour.
steps.tip: Dry flour on the surface burns and clouds the frying oil. Always oil the board for luchi.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a deep kadhai to 180C — a scrap of dough should rise to the surface within 2 seconds.
Slide in one luchi. It will sink, then float within 3 seconds.
Press the centre down gently with the back of a slotted spoon for 3-4 seconds and it will balloon.
steps.tip: That gentle press is the trick to a full puff — without it you get a flat disc.

steps.text: Flip and fry the second side 15 seconds only. Luchi should stay white and blond, never brown.
steps.tip: If they are colouring, your oil is too hot. Drop the heat between batches.

steps.text: Drain upright in a colander rather than flat on paper so they stay puffed.
Serve straight away with cholar dal or aloo dum.

storage: Luchi are at their best within 20 minutes. They will keep soft for a few hours in a covered container but will not re-puff; do not refrigerate.
